Definition 1.1. A (general) system is a relation on nonempty (abstract) sets
S ⊂ × Vᵢ : i ∈ I (2.1)
where × denotes Cartesian product and I is the index set. A component set Vᵢ is referred to as a system object. When I is finite, (2.1) is written in the form
S ⊂ V₁ × ⋯ × Vₙ (2.2)
rationale: The definition proper: named sorts (nonempty abstract sets Vᵢ, index set I) with the fixed relation S ⊂ ×{Vᵢ}; transcribable without adding content.
caveat: Starting point for the entire development is provided by the following definitions.

location: Chapter II, §1(a), Definition 1.2, book p. 11 = scan page 22; eq. (2.3)
passage:
Definition 1.2. Let Iₓ ⊂ I and Iᵧ ⊂ I be a partition of I, i.e., Iₓ ∩ Iᵧ = φ, Iₓ ∪ Iᵧ = I. The set X = × {Vᵢ : i ∈ Iₓ} is termed the input object, while Y = × {Vᵢ : i ∈ Iᵧ} is termed the output object. The system S is then
S ⊂ X × Y (2.3)
and will be referred to as an input–output system.
rationale: Defines the qualified variant the authors actually use throughout the book: components X and Y constructed from a partition of I, with the constraint S ⊂ X × Y.
caveat: The form (2.3) rather than (2.2) will be used throughout this book.

S : X → Y (2.4)
it is referred to as a function-type (or functional) system.

caveat: Which of the forms for S is used will be clear from the context in which it is used. Analogous comment applies to the use of the same symbol S in (2.3) and (2.4).
